alignment.note: ὁ δὲ / ܗܘ ܕܝܢ / At ille — articular subject plus adversative particle, equivalent across all three.

Greek and Latin render the aorist participle ἐξελθὼν / egressus as a single circumstantial participle; the Peshitta employs the subordinating particle ܟܕ ('when') plus finite verb ܢܦܩ, the characteristic Syriac periphrasis for Greek temporal participles.

Greek ἤρξατο and Latin cœpit are simple aorist/perfect forms; the Peshitta uses the analytic past ܫܪܝ ܗܘܐ with auxiliary ܗܘܐ to mark inceptive past, a regular Syriac construction lacking a direct one-word equivalent.
κηρύσσειν / ܡܟܪܙ / prædicare — 'to proclaim.'
Greek πολλὰ ('much/greatly') is matched by Syriac ܣܓܝ, but the Vulgate omits the adverbial intensifier entirely, leaving prædicare unqualified.
Coordinating conjunction καί / ܘ (prefixed) / et.

Greek διαφημίζειν ('to spread abroad') and Latin diffamare correspond; the Peshitta uses the verb from root ܛܘܒ (ܘܐܛܒܗ, 'and he made it widely known/noised abroad') which incorporates both the conjunction and a pronominal object suffix referring to the word.
τὸν λόγον / ܠܡܠܬܐ / sermonem — 'the word/matter,' the Syriac and Latin both carrying the definite/accusative force.
Result clause introducer ὥστε / ܐܝܟܢܐ / ita ut.

Greek μηκέτι is a single negative-temporal adverb ('no longer'); Syriac uses ܕܠܐ ('that not') and Latin splits the sense across jam non, each tradition distributing the 'no-longer' nuance differently.

Greek δύνασθαι (present infinitive) and Latin posset (imperfect subjunctive) are single verbs; the Peshitta renders ܢܫܟܚ ܗܘܐ with the auxiliary ܗܘܐ, again forming the analytic past potential characteristic of Syriac.

Greek uses the pronoun αὐτὸν ('he/him') as subject; the Peshitta makes the referent explicit by naming ܝܫܘܥ ('Jesus'), a typical Syriac clarification, while the Latin carries the subject implicitly within posset and supplies no separate token.
φανερῶς / ܓܠܝܐܝܬ / manifeste — 'openly.'
εἰς πόλιν εἰσελθεῖν / ܕܢܥܘܠ ܠܡܕܝܢܬܐ / introire in civitatem — 'to enter into [the] city.'
ἀλλ᾽ ἔξω / ܐܠܐ ܠܒܪ / sed foris — 'but outside.'

Greek ἐπ᾽ ἐρήμοις τόποις and Latin in desertis locis use the plural ('in solitary places'); the Peshitta ܒܐܬܪܐ ܚܘܪܒܐ employs the singular 'in (a) desert region,' a typical Syriac preference for the collective singular of geographic terms.
Copula/locative verb ἦν / ܗܘܐ / esset — 'he was.'
Coordinating καί / ܘ (prefixed) / et.

Greek ἤρχοντο (imperfect) and Latin conveniebant (imperfect) are single verbs of continuous action; the Peshitta ܘܐܬܝܢ ܗܘܘ uses the participle plus auxiliary ܗܘܘ to express the durative past, the standard Syriac equivalent of the Greek imperfect.
πρὸς αὐτὸν / ܠܘܬܗ / ad eum — 'to him,' the Syriac compressing preposition and pronoun into a single suffixed form.

Greek πάντοθεν and Latin undique are single adverbs meaning 'from every side'; the Peshitta paraphrases analytically with ܡܢ ܟܠ ܕܘܟܐ ('from every place'), expanding the adverb into a prepositional phrase as Syriac lacks a comparable one-word form.
